name: SoundSwitch
tagline: Software that drives DMX lighting rigs in sync with DJ software, with auto-generated and hand-timed light shows per track.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The output side is boring in a good way: DMX is a documented protocol, Art-Net is UDP packets, and a USB interface is a serial device, so an agent can absolutely make your lights move to a beat in one session. Beat-reactive scenes driven by a live audio input are a weekend project, and if you run rekordbox or Engine DJ you can pull real beat grid and track position off the network with existing reverse-engineered link libraries. What you cannot one-shot is the boring infrastructure around it: a fixture profile library covering thousands of cheap Chinese moving heads, a timeline editor that survives you dragging cues around at 1am, and autoloops that make a show look composed instead of strobing randomly. Serato in particular has no friendly hook, so per-track scripted shows mean either manual triggering or a sketchy workaround. Build it if your rig is eight fixtures you know the channel map for and you enjoy debugging DMX addressing; buy it if you are being paid to show up and have the lights work.
coreLoopDIY: Reads live audio or a DJ link stream for tempo and beats, then pushes beat-synced DMX frames to your fixtures over Art-Net or a USB interface with a few switchable scenes.
requirements: A USB-DMX interface (FTDI/Enttec Open DMX style) or an Art-Net node on the same network
Hand-written channel maps for each fixture you own, pulled from its manual
An audio input feeding the machine, or rekordbox/Engine DJ on the LAN for beat data
Willingness to test in a dark room before testing in front of people
whatYouLose: The fixture profile library, so every new light means reading a PDF and typing channel offsets
A real timeline editor for scripting shows to specific tracks, plus the autoloop generation that fakes good taste
Native hooks into Serato, Virtual DJ and Engine DJ, including track ID and position without network guesswork
First-party hardware like Control One and the DMX interfaces that are known to work under load
Crash resistance during a paid gig, which is the only reliability metric that matters here
moatNotes: Being owned by inMusic means the Engine DJ and Denon side of the integration is inside the house, not reverse engineered.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the thing being replaced is not the DMX math, it is the accumulated grunt work: a fixture library someone else maintained, DJ software integrations that would otherwise be packet sniffing projects, and hardware that has been beaten on at real events. A DIY controller that works in your living room is a genuinely fun build and a completely different risk profile from a rig you carry into a venue where the promoter is watching. Anyone getting paid to light a room tends to pay for software that fails less often than their own code.
notes: The protocol is trivial and the fixture library is not, which is the usual shape of this answer.
prompt:
Build a local, offline DMX lighting controller for a small DJ rig. No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack: Python 3.11. Use sounddevice for audio capture, numpy for analysis, a plain socket for Art-Net output, pyserial for USB-DMX output, and FastAPI plus a single static HTML page with htmx for the control UI. No database, config lives in YAML files.

In scope:
1. fixtures.yaml: a list of fixtures, each with name, dmx_start_address, and a channel map (e.g. dimmer, red, green, blue, pan, tilt, gobo) given as offsets from the start address.
2. scenes.yaml: named scenes. Each scene declares per-fixture target values plus an effect: static, pulse_on_beat, chase, or color_cycle. Include a beat_division field (1, 2, 4) so effects can fire on every beat, every other beat, or every bar.
3. A DMX output layer that maintains a 512-channel universe buffer and writes it at a steady 40 frames per second. Two backends, selected by an env var: ARTNET (UDP to ARTNET_HOST:6454, proper ArtDMX packet header) and SERIAL (Enttec Open DMX style break plus frame over SERIAL_PORT). Frame rate must not stutter when the UI is being used, so run output in its own thread.
4. A beat detector: capture the selected input device, compute a spectral flux onset envelope in short hops, track tempo with autocorrelation over a rolling window, and emit beat timestamps with a confidence value. When confidence drops below a threshold, fall back to a manual tap-tempo BPM.
5. A local web UI at 127.0.0.1:8080 showing current BPM, beat confidence, a beat blink indicator, buttons to switch scenes, a master dimmer slider, a tap tempo button, and a big blackout button that zeroes the universe immediately.
6. A --dry-run flag that prints a compact text visualisation of the universe instead of sending packets, so it can be developed without hardware.

Out of scope: no per-track scripted timelines, no Serato or rekordbox integration, no fixture profile library, no mobile app, no multi-universe support.

Put ARTNET_HOST, SERIAL_PORT, AUDIO_DEVICE and DMX_BACKEND in .env, loaded with python-dotenv, and commit a .env.example. Write a README with wiring notes, a worked fixtures.yaml example for a 4-channel RGB par and a 12-channel moving head, and a loud warning to test the blackout button before any real use.
